items.title: Snapdragons disprove Mendel's simplest law in one cross
items.claim: Red snapdragon crossed with white snapdragon. Mendel's dominance rule says: offspring should all be red (or all white). Snapdragon offspring are PINK. The textbook law fails on its very first test.

options.text: Mendel's laws don't apply to plants

Incomplete dominance — heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype because neither allele fully masks the other; the red allele encodes a pigment enzyme, and one functional copy produces only half as much pigment as two
Pink is a separate allele not from either parent

items.reveal:
Mendel happened to choose seven traits in peas that were all controlled by single genes with full dominance and complete penetrance. Most real traits are not.

Incomplete dominance: heterozygotes show intermediate phenotypes. Pink snapdragons. Pink camellias. Light pink human skin (one functional MC1R copy).

Codominance: both alleles fully expressed simultaneously. Human ABO blood group (a person with A and B alleles has both A and B antigens on red cells).

Epistasis: gene A's effect depends on gene B's genotype. Coat colour in Labradors (E gene controls whether B gene's brown/black is visible at all).

Polygenic inheritance: traits like height controlled by hundreds of small-effect genes. Family resemblance plus 'regression to the mean'.

Real genetics is much richer than 'dominant masks recessive'.
items.why: Mendel's laws are presented as universal. They describe a subset of inheritance patterns. Even simple breeding shows the laws don't always apply directly.

items.title: The avocado was made for a giant ground sloth
items.claim: Avocado fruit has a huge stone surrounded by lipid-rich flesh. No living mammal can swallow it whole. The fruit's design anticipated a disperser — likely the now-extinct Pleistocene megafauna (giant ground sloths, gomphotheres). The plant outlived its partner.
items.prompt: What does this tell us about coevolution?

options.text: Plants and dispersers shape each other's traits over millions of years; when the partner goes extinct, the plant may persist with traits that look maladaptive in the present — ecological 'ghosts of evolution past'
Plants don't need animals for dispersal
Coevolved plants always go extinct with their partners

items.reveal:
Daniel Janzen and Paul Martin (1982) proposed the concept of 'anachronistic fruits': fruits whose size, hardness, smell or chemistry seem designed for dispersers that no longer exist.

North American megafauna went extinct ~13,000 years ago (climate change plus human hunting): mastodons, giant ground sloths (up to 6 metres tall), gomphotheres, glyptodonts. Many large-fruited Central American trees — avocados, papayas, large legume pods — appear to have coevolved with these animals.

Without megafaunal dispersal, these trees rely on humans, water, or rare alternatives (jaguars eat avocados; tapirs swallow some seeds whole). Many would have declining ranges if not for human cultivation.

Osage orange (Maclura pomifera): grapefruit-sized fruits with little use to modern animals. Likely a mastodon plant. Now native to a small Texas range; spread widely only because humans use it as windbreaks and hedges.

Coffee, cacao, durian — all probably coevolved with mammalian dispersers and rely on living relatives or human cultivation for survival.

The broader point: present-day ecology contains relics from past ecologies. Some traits make sense only in the context of vanished species and lost interactions.
items.why: Coevolution implies tight mutual adaptation. When one partner disappears, the other can persist but appears strangely engineered for a world that no longer exists.

items.title: You are outnumbered by your own bacteria
items.claim: Adult humans carry about 38 trillion bacterial cells, roughly matching the count of human cells. By gene count, microbial DNA dwarfs human DNA by 100 to 1. They digest your food, train your immune system and affect your behaviour.

options.text: Humans have 10 times more bacteria than human cells
The ratio is closer to 1.3:1 (bacteria:human), based on revised counts (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016) — much closer than the older 10:1 figure suggested
There are about as many bacterial cells as human red blood cells
Bacterial cell count is roughly the same as human muscle cell count

items.reveal:
The famous 10:1 ratio came from a 1972 back-of-envelope estimate by Thomas Luckey. It propagated through textbooks for 40 years.

In 2016, Sender, Fuchs and Milo revisited the numbers. They estimated about 30 trillion human cells (84 percent red blood cells) and 38 trillion bacterial cells (most in the colon). The ratio is close to 1:1.

Gene count is a different story. Each human cell carries 20,000 genes; the gut microbiome contains an estimated 2 to 20 million unique microbial genes — so by gene count, we're 99 percent microbe.

The gut microbiome makes vitamins, ferments fibre, modulates the immune system and produces neurotransmitters that may affect mood and behaviour (the 'gut-brain axis').
items.why: Self/other has clear boundaries in popular imagination. Biologically, the boundary is fuzzy and statistical.
